text:
Illinois EPA’s Office of Energy is offering funding to support the state’s Priority Climate Action Plan, made possible through Climate Pollution Reduction Grant Implementation Funds. The Residential Electrification Catalyst Grant Program expands efforts to make residential buildings cleaner, healthier, and more energy efficient.

Through this program, Local Action Agencies (LAAs) and Community Action Agencies (CAAs) engaged in home weatherization can broaden their residential services to fill remaining electrification gaps—such as installing heat pumps, heat pump water heaters, and other necessary upgrades. This support complements existing state and federal incentives available to low‑income households and is specifically designed to address funding gaps in municipal and cooperative utility service areas.

Only LAAs and CAAs offering services in these eligible service areas may apply. As program implementers, these agencies will distribute funding to each home using the following structure:

Total funding requested cannot exceed the award amount received through the Illinois Home Weatherization Assistance Program (IHWAP).

Up to $20,000 per home is available and must include at least one electrification measure. Whole‑home electrification is encouraged, but must demonstrate modeled cost savings.

Funds must be braided with IHWAP, with 50% allocated to IHWAP and 50% allocated to the Residential Electrification Catalyst Grant Program.

Client eligibility is limited to households approved through the IHWAP application review process.

The Residential Electrification Catalyst Grant Program plays a critical role in helping Illinois accelerate its transition to cleaner, more resilient homes—particularly for residents who face the highest energy burdens. Despite the availability of federal and state incentives, many low‑income households remain unable to take full advantage of electrification upgrades due to limited funding, high upfront costs, and gaps in utility service availability. These barriers routinely lead to “walk‑aways,” where projects that would meaningfully improve health, comfort, and long‑term affordability simply cannot proceed.

By strategically supplementing existing programs like IHWAP, this initiative ensures that essential electrification measures—such as heat pumps and heat pump water heaters—can be installed where they would otherwise be out of reach. The program not only reduces greenhouse gas emissions but also supports energy equity, enabling more Illinois residents to access modern, efficient technologies that lower utility bills and improve indoor air quality.

In addition, focusing on municipal and cooperative utility service areas closes a long‑standing funding gap that has limited the reach of electrification programs. The Catalyst Grant strengthens coordination across agencies, supports implementers already trusted within communities, and helps Illinois meet its statewide climate goals through practical, household‑level impact.

title: Heinrich, Lee, Capito, and Whitehouse Introduce Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs ...
description:
This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, as well as targeted reforms for various energy projects.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also forces data centers to pay their fair share by requiring them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs.
It will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses.
If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” said Whitehouse.
text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senators Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Mike Lee (R-Utah), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Chairman of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), Ranking Member of the U.S. Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, introduced the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 to reform the federal environmental review and permitting process. This groundbreaking agreement will deliver cheaper energy, more jobs, and responsible growth across the United States.

The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act provides certainty that permitted energy and infrastructure projects will retain their permits absent extraordinary circumstances, violations of law, or court order, as well as targeted reforms for various energy projects. This legislation reflects input from members of Congress on both sides of the aisle and from a diverse group of stakeholders. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act also forces data centers to pay their fair share by requiring them to pay for all of their associated transmission costs.

“America is entering a new era of energy demand. We have an enormous opportunity to build big things again to meet this moment – to build more generation, expand our grid, create more jobs, lower energy costs, and make sure we have the energy we need to compete. It should not take decades to build the infrastructure our country needs,” said Heinrich. “Our Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will help us get to ‘yes’ or ‘no’ on energy projects faster, while protecting important environmental safeguards and protecting the ability of Tribes to formally consult during these processes. It will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses. And as data centers drive demand for more power, it will ensure they pay their fair share of the grid upgrades they require – not leave that bill to American families. Our bill puts teeth behind that principle.”

“We once built projects like the Hoover Dam, the Golden Gate Bridge, and the Empire State Building in years, not decades,” said Lee. “America still has the resources and the talent, but what too often stands in the way is a permitting system that takes too long and costs too much. After years of work in Congress and many months of negotiations, I’m proud we’ve reached a bipartisan agreement to fix this broken process and get America back to building.”

“For far too long, our broken and outdated federal environmental review and permitting processes have stood in the way of energy reliability, secure jobs, modern infrastructure, and economic growth. The bipartisan reforms we secured in this deal will transform our nation’s ability to power our economy and fuel future growth, while continuing to protect the land, water, and wildlife we all cherish. I look forward to working with our colleagues in the Senate and the House, and President Trump to get this essential legislation signed into law so we can build the infrastructure America needs to grow and thrive,” said Capito.

“The American people want lower energy bills, and they want more clean energy. Our permitting reform plan gets us a long way toward both of those goals. If we can pass this bill, we will flood the grid with clean, affordable energy and make data centers start paying their fair share,” said Whitehouse. “Like all major pieces of bipartisan legislation, this bill is a compromise. We believe it is a compromise that will result in a brighter, cleaner, more affordable future.”

text:
Two local environmental groups are criticizing the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality for its tardiness in identifying and penalizing Clean Air Act violations in the Lake Charles area, Louisiana Illuminator reports.

The Environmental Integrity Project and Micah 6:8 Mission reviewed LDEQ’s handling of violations at 23 facilities from January 2021 through August 2026 and identified delays in enforcement, heavy reliance on companies to self-report violations and warning letters and a lack of required corrective actions. Meanwhile, the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality argues the assessment is too broad and does not account for the agency’s recent steps toward more timely enforcement.

The groups found that LDEQ took an average of 1.7 years to issue 45 warning letters after reported incidents or inspections, with one taking 10 years. They cite cases involving the Phillips 66 Lake Charles refinery and Indorama Ventures Olefins in Westlake as examples of how delays can limit the state’s ability to require fixes or collect penalties.

The review found LDEQ took formal enforcement action 28 times during the period, but none of those cases included required corrective measures or investigations to determine the root causes of violations. The groups recommended clearer standards for escalating warning letters to formal enforcement, enforceable corrective measures and follow-up inspections.

LDEQ officials point to a 365-day deadline implemented following recommendations from a 2021 Legislative Auditor report, as well as 3,456 enforcement actions, including 975 related to air quality, during the review period. LDEQ says most cases were identified, evaluated and processed without the extended delays highlighted by the environmental groups and argues that enforcement timelines vary based on workload and case complexity.

text:
Democratic lawmakers are warning that the proposed $67 billion merger between NextEra Energy and Dominion Energy could reduce competition and raise electricity prices for consumers.

In a letter to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) on Wednesday, the legislators expressed concern that the enlarged company would have excessive market power, allowing it to pass costs on to ratepayers, defer upgrades on the energy grid and avoid scrutiny from federal regulators. The new company could also use its control over transmission lines to disadvantage rivals, according to the lawmakers.

FERC, a government agency, is responsible for ensuring mergers are consistent with the public interest.

"We urge you to closely scrutinize this merger and block it if the Commission determines it would increase market concentration or have an adverse effect on costs for consumers — or if the acquisition is otherwise not in the public interest," the lawmakers wrote in the Sept. 30 letter, shared exclusively with CBS News.

Signing the letter were Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts and Rep. Suhas Subramanyam of Virginia, who led the effort, as well as Sens. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut; Edward Markey of Massachusetts; Chris Murphy of Connecticut; Jack Reed and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island; and Reps. Chris Deluzio of Pennsylvania; Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire; Raja Krishnamoorthi of Illinois; Seth Magaziner of Rhode Island; and Eugene Vindman of Virginia.

NextEra and Dominion didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter.

Largest utility in the world

NextEra announced in May that it would acquire Dominion, saying the deal would create the "largest regulated electric utility" in the world. The merger is expected to close in mid- to late 2027.

The new company would serve around 10 million utility customers across Florida, North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia, and own all of the nuclear power plants in New England.

The companies have said they are committed to delivering affordable energy. In announcing the deal, NextEra also proposed offering $2.25 billion in bill credits to Dominion customers for two years following the merger's closing.

In their letter on Wednesday, the lawmakers said independent monitors have found that utility companies involved in mergers routinely tout rate reductions but often fail to deliver on savings.

"FERC should similarly be skeptical of promises for rate credits in this case," the legislators wrote.

title: Savings Alert: Central Coast Energy Bill Credits Happening Now - Robert Rivas
description:
This includes new protections to make sure Central Coast families aren’t footing the bill for large energy users like data centers and the costs they create.
Together, these measures strengthen protections for Central Coast ratepayers while helping make sure California’s energy system remains affordable, reliable and ready for the future.
So when utility companies save money, Central Coast ratepayers can benefit from those savings too.
Continuing to Stabilize Costs for Central Coast Communities For Central Coast families, the combination of immediate bill relief and longer-term reforms is part of a broader effort to make energy cleaner, more affordable and reliable.
From Salinas and Watsonville to Hollister, Monterey and communities throughout the Central Coast, families are feeling the pressure of higher everyday costs.
text:
It’s the season for savings on your energy bills, thanks to the work of California Democrats at the state Capitol.

This year, California lawmakers delivered new ways to put money back in the pockets of Central Coast homeowners and ratepayers. These important solutions prevent rising energy costs from being shifted onto working families, and make sure profits go back to families and business owners, not major corporations.

This includes new protections to make sure Central Coast families aren’t footing the bill for large energy users like data centers and the costs they create. New laws also increase transparency around how utility rates and profits are determined and require utilities to pass any savings on to customers.

Together, these measures strengthen protections for Central Coast ratepayers while helping make sure California’s energy system remains affordable, reliable and ready for the future.

Saving Money on Energy Bills Now

During the latest two-year legislative session, Speaker Robert Rivas and Assembly Democrats made stabilizing energy costs a central part of their work — delivering new protections for ratepayers, holding utility companies accountable and making sure California’s clean energy investments translate into real savings for families.

Now, that work is delivering money directly to Californians’ pockets — and you’ll see those savings on your latest bills.

Millions of households served by Pacific Gas & Electric and other major utilities are receiving an average of $75 in California Climate Credits this August and September — automatically saving a total of $886 million.

For Central Coast communities across Monterey, Santa Cruz, San Benito and southern Santa Clara counties, the credits provide direct relief during the months when electricity use and bills can rise.

The California Climate Credit is one of the most direct ways California is returning money to households.

The credits come from the state’s Cap-and-Invest program and are being provided automatically to eligible residential customers of PG&E, Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric. These credits are being delivered in August and September, when higher summer temperatures can drive up electricity use and monthly bills.

For a Central Coast family, that means an average of $75 in direct savings on their electricity bills this summer — without filling out an application or navigating a government program.

This relief builds on legislation advanced under Speaker Rivas’ leadership last year that is expected to return approximately $3 billion annually in Climate Credits to California households, while also investing in wildfire prevention, clean transportation, affordable housing and other priorities.

Holding Utility Companies Accountable

Bigger rebates on electricity bills, less pollution, more reliable power, new jobs, billions of dollars in energy savings for California — this legislative session, Assembly Democrats have continued to focus on affordable and sustainable energy solutions.

AB 2589 by Assemblymember Jacqui Irwin, signed by Governor Newsom on September 27, requires investor-owned utilities to pass certain savings resulting from changes in federal tax law on to their customers. So when utility companies save money, Central Coast ratepayers can benefit from those savings too.

The Assembly also advanced AB 2463 by Assemblymember Cottie Petrie-Norris, which increases transparency and accountability around how utility profits are determined, giving ratepayers a clearer view into how electricity and gas rates are set.

Together, these measures strengthen the Assembly’s efforts to make sure utility customers are given greater protection and a greater share of the savings.

Making Sure Data Centers Pay

Speaker Rivas and the Assembly have taken landmark steps to prevent the rapid growth of large energy users from driving up costs for everyone else.

AB 2383, authored by Assemblymember Rick Chavez Zbur, was signed into law on September 21, requiring large energy-use facilities to bear the costs associated with the electricity and infrastructure needed to serve them, helping prevent those costs from being shifted onto consumers and families.

The legislation is especially important as the growing artificial intelligence industry demands more energy use for data centers and other big corporate energy users. Rather than asking families and small businesses to absorb these costs, the new law requires large energy users to pay their fair share.

Other legislation advancing California’s energy affordability goals includes AB 2493, authored by Assemblymember Cottie Petrie-Norris, which would help connect affordable housing, health facilities and other community projects to power faster — bringing new power online and reducing costs associated with lengthy delays.

Continuing to Stabilize Costs for Central Coast Communities

For Central Coast families, the combination of immediate bill relief and longer-term reforms is part of a broader effort to make energy cleaner, more affordable and reliable.

From Salinas and Watsonville to Hollister, Monterey and communities throughout the Central Coast, families are feeling the pressure of higher everyday costs.

The Assembly’s energy affordability agenda is designed to meet that reality with tangible results: money returned directly to utility bills, stronger protections for ratepayers, greater accountability for utility companies and a more reliable energy system that can help control costs over the long term.

title: Tackling Environmental, Social, and Governance Risks to Boost Green Energy Finance
description:

“Large-scale renewable energy and grid infrastructure requires a significant increase in capital investments,” said Verena Hagg of Austria’s Finance Ministry.
The emphasis was on practitioners sharing knowledge and learning from one another, with case studies demonstrating that many risks within energy projects are common across organizations and countries.
More than 40% of infrastructure projects face delays, often caused by opposition over environmental and social concerns.

text:
A government seeks private funding for a solar plant to help address the country’s vital energy needs. The location is an area of vulnerable households and nomadic groups, near nesting grounds for endangered birds and an important cultural heritage site. To feed the electricity to the grid, a transmission line will have to be built through a densely populated area.

Would you invest in the project?

The scenario – fictional but based on real-life cases – was part of an interactive role-play by participants in Navigating Environmental, Social and Governance and Sustainability-linked Finance for the Energy Transition, a workshop hosted in Vienna by the Vienna Development Knowledge Center from September 15-17, 2026.

Some $2 trillion in investment will be needed every year until 2035 to fund the energy transition in emerging markets and developing economies – mostly private finance.

“Large-scale renewable energy and grid infrastructure requires a significant increase in capital investments,” said Verena Hagg of Austria’s Finance Ministry. “Public financing possibilities are increasingly limited, and this capital must therefore be mobilized from private commercial and institutional investors.”

While strong management of environmental, social and governance (ESG) risks in sustainable energy projects can ensure they do not cause unacceptable harm to people or habitats, it is increasingly also seen as a way to make projects attractive to investors, helping developers access broader pools of capital and build confidence among lenders and other stakeholders. It can also unlock more favourable financing terms such as lower bond coupon rates or longer repayment periods.

“Strong environmental and social performance is a critical enabler of sustainable finance and investment, ultimately supporting energy security and resilience and accelerating the transition to a more sustainable energy future,” said Ana Cristina Sanchez Thorin of the International Finance Corporation (IFC).

Putting ESG at the core of investment decision-making

The Vienna workshop brought together experts from across the World Bank Group – the World Bank, IFC, and Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency (MIGA) – working on environmental and social risk management, energy, infrastructure, and sustainable finance. Participants were drawn from the public and private sector across Europe and Central Asia, including ministries and regulators, state-owned enterprises, international financial institutions, commercial banks, investors, and private energy companies.

The emphasis was on practitioners sharing knowledge and learning from one another, with case studies demonstrating that many risks within energy projects are common across organizations and countries. Discussions explored how to make clean energy projects bankable from an ESG perspective; how ESG risks are actually assessed and managed throughout the project lifecycle; how financiers look at energy projects; how sustainable finance markets and financial instruments are evolving; and the practical experience of developers implementing ESG requirements on the ground. Field trips to a hydro-electric plant and a wind farm operated by Austria’s leading power company, Verbund, provided an opportunity to discuss ESG initiatives in practice.

The cost of poor ESG practices can be very high. More than 40% of infrastructure projects face delays, often caused by opposition over environmental and social concerns. In Europe and Central Asia alone, a dam project has been blocked for decades by resistance to the planned displacement of over 2,000 residents and flooding of cultural heritage sites, while opposition to electricity transmission corridors in another country has caused significant cost increases and construction delays, hampering national plans to scale up renewable energy. One wind power project attracted protests after it failed to consider nomadic groups who used the land; others have raised controversy over dangers to birds and bats.

Multiple examples showed that environmental and social issues are often easier and less costly to address when identified early in project preparation, rather than after financing decisions have been made or construction has begun.

“These issues can lead to financing being cancelled, in addition to serious reputational issues for investors, sponsors and developers,” said the World Bank’sHelene Carlsson Rex. “Doing this right gets projects built on time, better financed and upholds the social license to operate.”

Harmonizing ESG frameworks

Presenters outlined various frameworks for ESG due diligence: the World Bank’s Environmental and Social Standards; the Environmental and Social Performance Standards used by the IFC and MIGA; the European Union’s Taxonomy of environmentally sustainable activities; the United Nations Development Programme’s Social and Environmental Standards; and the Hydropower Sustainability Alliance’s Hydropower Sustainability Standard.

These typically cover requirements across a wide range of areas, including working conditions; health and safety; pollution; biodiversity; land acquisition and resettlement; transparency and stakeholder engagement; and protections for indigenous peoples and cultural heritage.

While different ESG frameworks may vary in terminology and specific requirements, there is growing alignment around core principles, including early identification of environmental and social risks, meaningful stakeholder engagement, strong governance, and effective mitigation planning. This makes it easier for projects and investors to follow and adhere to standards.

The World Bank Group is working to harmonize its environmental and social requirements too, updating the Performance Standards applied to the private sector so that as far as possible they mirror the public sector framework. The United Nations is moving towards a common approach to environmental and social standards for all UN programs, and a comparison by the IFC and EU of their respective frameworks has concluded that they are already quite well aligned.

As well as standards, effective ESG management also depends on governance, institutional capacity, and clear accountability mechanisms that allow organizations to translate commitments into day-to-day implementation. Investors assess not only the risks in themselves, but the capacity of project sponsors and developers to understand, manage, and implement solutions throughout the project lifecycle. Confidence in a project’s preparation, governance arrangements, and ability to deliver on ESG commitments can often be just as important as the specific framework applied.

“Environmental and social aspects are key to bankability,” said the World Bank’s Sanjay Srivastava. “The correct management of these aspects is critical to attract private capital, which is needed to close the energy gap.”

So, did participants finance the fictional solar plant? Would-be investors were wary of unaddressed ESG risks, saying they would need more information on a slew of factors, from threats to biodiversity and livelihoods, through to costs, potential alternative sites, and plans for stakeholder engagement and risk mitigation.

“As of now, we can’t commit to anything,” they said – a perfect illustration that environmental and social risks are easiest to address early, when they can strengthen both project outcomes and investor confidence.

name: Louisiana and Evs
title: U.S. electricity use for electric vehicles increasing at a slower pace in 2026
description:
The slowing electric vehicle electricity consumption growth followed a decline in sales after U.S. federal tax credits expired in September 2025.
Overall, U.S. light-duty electric vehicle electricity use has more than doubled since 1H23, totaling nearly 14 billion kilowatthours in 1H26.
Both battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles can consume electricity from the grid and are included in our electric vehicle electricity consumption estimates.
Internal combustion, hybrid electric, and fuel cell electric vehicles consume other fuels, do not connect to the grid, and are not included in our electric vehicle electricity use data.
In 2024, the most recent year of available data, electric vehicles accounted for 2% of all registered light-duty vehicles in the United States.
text:
We estimate light-duty electric vehicles in the United States consumed 8% more electricity during the first six months of 2026 than in the last half of 2025 (2H25) in our Monthly Energy Review, down from the 13–24% growth seen in six-month periods in recent years. The slowing electric vehicle electricity consumption growth followed a decline in sales after U.S. federal tax credits expired in September 2025. Overall, U.S. light-duty electric vehicle electricity use has more than doubled since 1H23, totaling nearly 14 billion kilowatthours in 1H26.

Americans drive many different vehicle types. Both battery electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles can consume electricity from the grid and are included in our electric vehicle electricity consumption estimates. Internal combustion, hybrid electric, and fuel cell electric vehicles consume other fuels, do not connect to the grid, and are not included in our electric vehicle electricity use data.

The New Clean Vehicle Credit and Qualified Commercial Clean Vehicle Credit, which reduced the cost to buy and lease new electric vehicles, ended on September 30, 2025. In 1H26, new electric vehicle sales were down 19% compared with 2H25. New electric vehicle sales are relatively small compared with the total number of vehicles on the road. In 2024, the most recent year of available data, electric vehicles accounted for 2% of all registered light-duty vehicles in the United States.

Our electric vehicle electricity consumption data are estimates for on-road, light-duty vehicles that weigh less than or equal to 8,500 pounds. We do not collect these data on our traditional surveys. Instead, we estimate electric vehicle electricity use with a recently finalized model based on external data sources. Going forward we will continue to estimate these data series in our Monthly Energy Review and State Energy Data System.

text:
(The Center Square) – The American Energy Alliance praised the Trump Administration’s finalization of the “Freedom Means Affordable Cars” rule that will reset the Corporate Average Fuel Economy standards, thereby reducing costs for American families and causing safer roads.

“President Trump should be commended for upending the abuses of the [Corporate Average Fuel Economy] program by the Obama and Biden administrations,” President of the American Energy Alliance Tom Pyle said in a statement obtained by The Center Square.

Pyle said that the Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE) standards are “a relic of a bygone era when scarcity was dictating energy policy.”

According to the U.S. Department of Transportation, CAFE was enacted in 1975 and was intended to “reduce energy consumption by increasing the fuel economy of cars and light trucks.”

Pyle stated that “Washington has no place being in the business of deciding what kind of car Americans can buy.

“This rule offers a significant improvement, allowing manufacturers to work on actual fuel efficiency innovation rather than relying on EV mandates or complicated fleetwide accounting,” Pyle said.

“But as long as the government has the authority to mandate fuel efficiency, the ability of future administrations to further disrupt auto markets will persist,” Pyle said. “It’s time for Congress to repeal CAFE altogether.”

When reached for comment, the Department of Transportation referred The Center Square to a news release.

U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said in the release: “Thanks to President Trump’s leadership, we have finally ended the illegal mandate that forced automakers to produce more expensive electric vehicles that American families didn’t want.”

“With our commonsense standards in place, we are making the American dream affordable again, putting safer cars on the road, and investing in the American autoworker,” Duffy said.

The American Energy Alliance’s Tom Pyle noted that “most importantly,” the reset of CAFE is “about affordability and choice.”

“With projected savings of roughly $1,300 per vehicle, families should have a little more wiggle room in their budgets and more freedom to buy the cars and trucks that actually fit their lives, their work, and their needs, not the vehicles that politicians and bureaucrats think they should drive,” Pyle said.

“Ending the credit-trading scheme, which effectively shifted costs onto buyers of standard vehicles while benefiting EV manufacturing, is especially important,” Pyle said.

“Additionally, these changes give automakers greater certainty and make it harder for future administrations to abruptly reverse course,” Pyle said.

text:
“The EPA's Data Center Disaster” Report (PDF)

Washington (September 30, 2026) - Senator Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.), member of the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee and the Environment and Public Works Committee, today released a report titled, The EPA’s Data Center Disaster: How the Trump Administration is Destroying Environmental Protections and Selling Out Communities for Big Tech, detailing the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)’s campaign of reckless deregulation to dilute environmental and public health guardrails in direct service of Big Tech’s race to build data centers.

“75% of Americans do not want a data center in their backyard, yet Trump’s EPA has chosen to facilitate data center construction at the expense of our health, our pocketbooks, and our bedrock environmental laws. In what they have coined as ‘the largest deregulatory agenda in American history,’ President Trump and EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin have issued rollbacks of air, water, and toxic chemical regulations that make it easier to build data centers and fossil fuel infrastructure to power them,” said Senator Markey. “Instead of subverting the EPA to Big Tech’s control, Trump and Zeldin should act in the interest of the American people and hold accountable the industries they are obligated to regulate. The public deserves an EPA that lives up to its name.”

Senator Markey’s report pulls back the curtain on the EPA’s abuse of power and failure to fulfill its mission of protecting human health and the environment. Since January 2025, Trump’s EPA has proposed and finalized rollbacks to undermine longstanding public health guardrails, explicitly and repeatedly naming data centers as a key beneficiary. And beyond these individual regulatory rollbacks, Zeldin has refused to contemplate any nationwide standards for data centers, despite increasing evidence of the harm that data centers and their related power infrastructure inflict on U.S. communities.

The cost of unfettered data center buildout is a real, present danger to the public. Air pollution associated with data centers in the United States caused an estimated $6.7 billion in public-health costs in 2023 and is projected to reach $20 billion by 2028. The EPA’s deregulatory blitz will only exacerbate this harm as communities have less protection and less input.

Senator Markey has been the leading voice against irresponsible and unregulated data center buildout at the expense of public health and the environment.

In July, Senator Markey released a discussion draft of his Protecting Communities Against Data Center Impacts proposal, a bill that would create a national framework to prevent increased energy costs, pollution, and adverse health harms related to the rapid buildout of data centers and associated fossil fuel infrastructure.

In June, Senator Markey wrote to EPA Administrator Zeldin to demand the withdrawal of a proposed rule that undermines Clean Air Act permitting standards to facilitate the buildout of data centers and associated fossil fuel infrastructure.

In June, Senator Markey reintroduced his Artificial Intelligence (AI) Environmental Impacts Act, legislation that would require data center operators to report the full range of their facilities’ environmental impacts.

In November 2025, Senator Markey wrote to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) urging the agency to ensure that increased and projected energy demand from data centers does not result in unjust or unreasonable rate hikes for American households.

In September 2025, Senator Markey wrote to the EPA in opposition to the agency’s initial announcement of plans to roll back the NSR program for data center buildout.

In July 2025, Senator Markey hosted a roundtable discussion titled The Data Center Next Door: Hidden Costs and Harms of Artificial Intelligence and Cryptomining to highlight the adverse environmental, health, climate, and energy cost impacts of data center proliferation in communities across the United States, and to condemn the deregulatory actions set forth in President Trump’s AI Action Plan. On the day of the roundtable, Senator Markey also released a storybook to spotlight the experiences of American families living with data centers in their backyard.

text:
1.3 GWp of new solar power — enough clean electricity to meet the annual needs of more than 280,000 households, close to one million people.

€100 million from the EIB is helping turn a €728 million investment into a major new pillar of Romania’s energy security.

1,500+ jobs, an 82-hectare nature reserve and investment in a Cohesion region — making Dama Solar about more than clean power.

The European Investment Bank (EIB) is providing €100 million for Dama Solar, a new large-scale solar power plant being developed by Rezolv Energy in Arad County, western Romania. The total investment is estimated at €728 million.

With a planned peak capacity of around 1.3 gigawatts (GW), Dama Solar will be one of Europe’s largest solar power plants. Once operational, it is expected to produce enough electricity each year to meet the needs of more than 280,000 households – equivalent to close to one million people.

The plant will be connected to Romania’s high-voltage electricity network, allowing the solar power it produces to enter the national grid. By adding a large new source of renewable electricity, the project will help Romania produce more of its own clean energy and strengthen its energy security.

“Europe needs more clean energy, and it needs it at scale. Dama Solar will add a major new source of renewable electricity to Romania’s energy system while bringing investment and jobs to the region,” said EIB Vice-President Ioannis Tsakiris. “It is a good example of how European investment can support energy security, climate action and regional development together.”

The project is located in Arad County, one of Romania’s cohesion regions, where it is expected to create a peak workforce of around 1,500 jobs over the next three years. Construction and related work will also generate additional economic activity in the area.

Dama Solar will combine the solar plant with an 82-hectare area dedicated to nature restoration. Parts of the lower-quality agricultural land will be returned to pasture, with sheep used to manage vegetation. The area will help restore degraded steppe grassland and provide habitat for wildlife and protected bird species.

“We are extremely pleased to reach the financing milestone on this landmark project. The EIB team have done a fantastic job working with our other relationship lenders to deliver this transaction on an extremely aggressive timetable. EIB’s anchor ticket supported by Invest EU has played a crucial role in underpinning the wider financing package,” said, Head of Financing at Rezolv Energy Jan Viton.

The project has secured two 15-year Contracts for Difference for 520 MW of its capacity. The balance of the electricity produced by Dama Solar is planned to be supplied to market and to commercial and industrial customers through long-term agreements, giving businesses access to more renewable electricity.

The project supports Romania’s efforts to expand renewable energy, reduce greenhouse gas emissions and strengthen energy security. It is also aligned with the EIB’s priorities for renewable energy, climate action and investment in less-developed regions.

Background information

EIB Group

The European Investment Bank (ElB) Group is the financing arm of the European Union, owned by the 27 Member States, and one of the largest multilateral development banks in the world. In 2025, the EIB Group signed €100 billion of new financing and advisory services for over 870 high-impact projects in eight core priorities that support EU policy objectives: climate action and the environment, digitalisation and technological innovation, security and defence, territorial cohesion, agriculture and the bioeconomy, social infrastructure, strong global partnerships and the savings and investment union. Beyond long-term loans for large infrastructure, the EIB Group crowds in private investment for high-risk innovative projects and businesses, with a growing role in Europe’s markets for venture debt, venture capital, guarantees and securitisations.

The European Investment Fund (EIF) is the subsidiary of the EIB Group specialised in providing guarantees, securitisation and equity to improve access to finance for small and medium-sized businesses and startups across Europe. Acting as an anchor investor, through its extensive network of partnering banks and investment funds, the EIF mobilises private investment and nurtures the ecosystem of venture capital funds to support innovative European entrepreneurs.

With the support of all 27 EU governments, the EIF has joined forces with institutional investors in a pan-European alliance to mobilise up to €80 billion for investment into innovative companies scaling up to become global leaders. The joint effort will expand the size and scope of the highly successful European Tech Champions Initiative, which has helped create 15 European mega-funds and scale 45 companies, including 12 unicorns, since being established three years ago.

High-quality, up-to-date photos of our headquarters for media use are available here.

About Rezolv Energy

Launched in 2022 by Actis, a leading growth market investor in sustainable infrastructure, Rezolv Energy is an independent renewable energy producer with a 2.8GW portfolio of large-scale renewable energy projects in operation, construction or late-stage development across Southeastern Europe.

The company is focused on delivering clean, reliable and affordable electricity while supporting the energy transition and creating lasting environmental, social and economic value in the communities where it operates.

text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

General Motors’ Ultium Cells LLC joint venture with LG Energy Solution plans to upgrade its operations in Spring Hill, Tennessee, for the production of lithium manganese rich battery cells. Together with the supplier’s improvements toward production of lithium iron phosphate cells for energy storage systems, it represents a $1 billion investment by 2030, according to a press release.

Ultium Cells says that the facility will be the first in the world to mass-produce prismatic LMR cells — with a potential 33% boost in energy density versus lithium iron phosphate, which is the preferred affordable battery chemistry at present. Spring Hill will produce LFP and LMR chemistries, in both pouch and prismatic formats.

“Establishing LMR prismatic cell production at Ultium Cells in Spring Hill is a key step in GM’s strategy to match the right battery technology to customer needs and strengthen our leadership in domestic battery manufacturing and innovation,” said Kurt Kelty, GM vice president of battery and sustainability.

Dive Insight:

Significant improvements in energy density in a chemistry intended for affordability means that future EVs might be able to add driving range without adding cost — and, perhaps, while cutting weight.

As the International Energy Agency pointed out in its most recent Global EV Outlook, LFP battery packs tend to be 40% cheaper on average compared to lithium manganese cobalt oxide alternatives on a kWh basis. But the lower energy density of LFP means higher weight, as NMC batteries tend to offer roughly 40% better energy density.

LMR cells are a lithium-ion chemistry that uses a higher percentage of lower-cost manganese in place of cobalt. And with the one-third better energy density versus LFP that Ultium Cells cites, they’re now close to the performance of NMC, but at a lower cost.

Ultium cells says that facility modifications are expected to be completed by 2028. GM had previously said that it intended to start production of LMR cells in the U.S. by 2028 for full-size electric trucks and SUVs.

“High-nickel batteries will continue to give customers the highest range in our portfolio, while adding LMR positions us to leapfrog today’s more affordable chemistries and deliver lower costs with better performance,” said Kelty. “This flexibility allows us to scale efficiently, reach more customers, and support GM’s long-term EV strategy and profitability journey.”

The shift to LMR cells might also help allow battery affordability without business ties to China. About 60% of the cells used for EVs globally are prismatic, according to the IEA — the format Ultium Cells plans to use for its LMR cells. Globally LFP batteries now account for about 55% of the global EV battery market, and China’s Contemporary Amperex Technology Co. and BYD Co. control the vast majority of supply and accompanying manufacturing capacity. That’s forced Western companies to license from these companies, which Ford Motor Co. has done with CATL, or form joint ventures.

Ultium Cells says that the necessary modifications to the facility will start later this year, with completion due in 2028. It’s expected to create 500 jobs, according to the company, in addition to the current workforce of 1,200.
